speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These amendments strengthen our levers against syndicates that organise and facilitate prostitution or "vice syndicates".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Vice syndicates have exploited technology to transform the way they operate, with apps and websites making it easier and more discreet than ever to: (a) advertise sexual services; (b) communicate with one another and with prospective clients; and (c) arrange payment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: What this means is that: syndicates can now remotely control their operations from anywhere in the world; they can introduce layers in their operations to evade detection but retain command and control by using these e-communication and e-payment platforms; and they can easily move from one residential unit to another, by renting these units to be used as "pop-up brothels".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This has brought about disamenities in the neighbourhoods and has made it more challenging for law enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: My first example is a typical experience faced by neighbours of units used for vice. "Mdm Jane" and her neighbours observed many unfamiliar male visitors going in and out of one of their neighbours’ units.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Imagine what "Mdm Jane" must have felt to see these men loitering near her home and the impact on her sense of safety for her teenage daughter. "Mdm Jane" made a Police report, and Police enforcement uncovered two females providing sexual services within the unit.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: My second example highlights some of the challenges faced by law enforcement because of changes in the syndicates’ modus operandi.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Last year, the Singapore Police Force and China's Ministry of Public Security conducted simultaneous raids across multiple locations in Singapore and China.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They arrested 36 syndicate members, including the key masterminds and agents based in China.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This led to the disruption of a major vice website targeting clients in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: While the Police could previously focus their resources to dismantle vice syndicates operating within certain areas of Singapore, now, these syndicates are all over the world.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is increasingly difficult and complicated to dismantle these syndicates and requires significant collaboration with foreign agencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We need to do more to address the rise in online vice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: So, it is necessary to strengthen our levers against vice syndicates and individuals, especially those operating through online means.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will also ensure better protection for our neighbourhoods against vice activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I will now go through the key amendments of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The first amendment targets syndicates that attempt to evade enforcement by moving parts of their operations overseas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, it is an offence under section 146A if a person in Singapore operates or maintains in Singapore a remote communication service to offer or facilitate the provision of sexual services in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But a webmaster in Singapore who relies on an overseas server to host his website to deliver sexual services in Singapore, would not run afoul of this section today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 10 amends section 146A so that it has extraterritorial application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The offence will be extended extraterritorially in two ways.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, it will apply to persons based outside Singapore, and second, it will apply to persons who use platforms based overseas, for example, a person in Singapore using a website server based overseas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In order for the extended offence to be made out, two conditions must be met.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, the remote communication service has to be used to offer or facilitate the provision, by a woman or girl, of sexual services in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, the remote communication service has to have a Singapore-link, namely, that a person physically present in Singapore is capable of having access to matters communicated using that service.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This extraterritorial application for section 146A will allow the Police to more effectively target transnational vice syndicates.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, the Bill increases penalties for vice offences in Part XI of the Women's Charter so as to more appropriately reflect the seriousness of these offences, and to better deter vice activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, higher maximum fines to match the profits derived from vice crimes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill, therefore, raises the maximum fines, to take into account the potential earnings of syndicates, and also inflation over the years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, longer maximum jail terms to raise the sentencing benchmarks for vice offences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, heavier penalties for second and subsequent conviction, for all vice-related offences in Part XI of the Women's Charter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, only some offences carry heavier penalties for re-offending.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But given the severity of vice offences, we need to take a stronger stand to better deter repeat offenders, regardless of their role in the conduct or delivery of the vice activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For the less serious offences, such as an offence committed by an owner whose place was used as a brothel under section 148, on first conviction, a maximum jail term of five years, or a maximum fine of $100,000, or both.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is up from the current maximum jail term of three years, or maximum fine of $3,000, or both.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is up from the current maximum jail term of five years, or maximum fine of $10,000, or both.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is up from the current mandatory maximum jail term of five years, and a discretionary maximum fine of $10,000.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: On second or subsequent conviction, a mandatory jail term of up to 10 years, and a discretionary maximum fine of $150,000.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is up from the current discretionary maximum fine of $10,000; there is no change to the current maximum jail term.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Police frequently receive complaints from the neighbours of such residential units.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: No one wants vice activities in their blocks or even on their streets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 12 makes it clearer in law the responsibilities of owners, tenants and other parties involved in the lease of any premises.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is necessary because syndicates commonly exploit the lack of checks at the point of leasing by misusing identity documents, in order to secure premises for vice activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, there have been cases of syndicates using false identities, and even a deceased person’s identity documents, to rent a property.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such misuse is problematic also because it makes it harder for the Police to track down the offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We want to deprive vice syndicates of operating space and safeguard the tranquility and safety of our neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To do so, we need the vigilance of three key stakeholders: (a) owners who rent out their properties; (b) tenants who rent from the landlords and sublet the premises to someone else; and (c) property agents who facilitate these lease and sublease transactions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A similar amendment is made to subsection (2) for tenants, lessees, occupiers or persons in charge of a place.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Property owners and tenants should also start asking the right questions when they rent out their properties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, who are the people they are letting the place to?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Will these people be staying there, or will they be allowing other parties to use the place?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Responsible property owners and tenants would already be asking these questions today when leasing out their premises.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These amendments simply provide more clarity to all owners and tenants on what they should do.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To help property owners and tenants understand what constitutes "reasonable diligence", we have included two illustrations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, owners and tenants should conduct identity checks of a prospective tenant or subtenant and the purpose of the tenancy or subtenancy, through face-to-face interviews, before leasing the place.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This can help ensure that the person they are transacting with is, indeed, who he or she claims to be and is not misusing another person’s identity document.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, if the owner is overseas, he should engage an agent or trusted person to conduct these face-to-face interviews on his behalf.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The owner should verify that the agent or trusted person has, indeed, carried out these checks.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These illustrations serve as guides to property owners and tenants.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, whether "reasonable diligence" was exercised would eventually depend on the specific facts of the case.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, if a property owner had already been warned by the Police that his flat could have been used as a brothel, the owner might be expected to do more to ensure that no brothel is operating at that flat.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We have consulted stakeholders extensively in developing this proposal, so that property owners and tenants are not overly burdened, while still ensuring that they exercise responsibility over their premises, and that they play their part in deterring syndicates from using their premises for vice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There is already a statutory requirement under the Immigration Act, for property owners to conduct identity checks of foreign tenants to ensure that there is no harbouring of immigration offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This has been in place since 1993, and property owners have largely complied.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These amendments are intended to get property owners to extend the identity checks to Singapore Citizen and Permanent Resident (PR) tenants and subtenants as well, so as to guard against premises being misused for vice activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The large majority of property owners and tenants who are law-abiding and acting in good faith will not have to worry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In each case, the Police will conduct investigations to establish the facts and take enforcement actions only where warranted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Property agents also have a critical role in keeping our neighbourhoods safe.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They should discharge their professional duties responsibly, and these are aligned to the reasonable diligence that we expect of property owners who lease out their premises, and tenants who sublet.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Property agents should guide property owners and tenants on what should be done in exercising reasonable diligence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: And, if property agents detect any suspicious transactions themselves, they should proactively document and report the matter to the Police.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We are working with the Council for Estate Agencies (CEA) to provide guidelines to the industry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Last month, I met with representatives from the industry to have a dialogue on these upcoming changes, and they gave many useful suggestions on how we can partner the industry to keep vice out of neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Where agents are found to have been negligent in carrying out their professional duties, they may be liable for regulatory action by CEA under the Estate Agents Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For instance, if the property agent does not comply with his or her professional duties which will include conducting identity checks on the parties involved in the lease transactions, the property agent may be penalised monetarily or have his or her registration suspended or revoked by CEA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: More critically, errant property agents who intentionally facilitate any lease transaction with the knowledge that it would lead to vice activities at the premises, are likely to face prosecution for abetting the commission of an offence under the Women's Charter, or other relevant laws.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Lastly, we are making some miscellaneous amendments to ensure that Police enforcement remains effective against the changing modus operandi of vice syndicates.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, a brothel is defined as a place that is used by at least two women or girls, whether at the same time or at different times, for the purposes of prostitution.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Syndicates have transformed the way they conduct their business, so that they circumvent the current definition of brothel, and avoid getting caught for vice offences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Earlier, I mentioned that syndicates would rent various residential units and shift from one to another to evade detection, effectively functioning as a "pop-up".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Each of these sex workers may also present herself as a lone operator.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These new modus operandi make it harder to prove that the premises are being used as brothels, as currently defined, even though it is clear from advertisements online that they are being used for prostitution.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We are, therefore, amending the definition of a "brothel" to enable the Police to take effective and decisive enforcement action.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 2 also simplifies the onus of proof on the part of the prosecution seeking to prove that a place is being used as a brothel.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The clause makes clear an existing practice on the use of indirect evidence to prove that a place is being used as a brothel.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, chat logs of appointments being made for prostitution services to be provided at the place would be allowed to be submitted as evidence that a place is being used as a brothel.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, only agents who bring into Singapore, receive or harbour a woman or girl who has been procured are liable for the offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The amendment will allow the Police to arrest a pimp or agent, even if the woman or girl is a freelance sex worker and, therefore, cannot be said to have been "procured" by anyone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is to make clear that our intent is to also target syndicates that use such a service, for example, vice agents who rely on messaging platforms provided by an Internet intermediary, and not the company operating and maintaining the service, such as telecommunications companies and Internet Service Providers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will enable the Police to also exercise powers of arrest with respect to syndicate members who use a remote communication service for the provision of sexual services.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To conclude, this Bill is part of our larger vice management strategy, which includes working with our partners on upstream education and deterrence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: (In Mandarin)  : 	These amendments are necessary to strengthen our levers against vice activities, in particular, against increasingly widespread online vice activities that have caused disamenities in our neighbourhoods and disturbances to the residents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: While Government agencies actively investigate these cases to prevent vice activities from taking root in our neighbourhoods, all of us have a part to play.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As property owners, we must stay vigilant when renting out our premises and not wait until after leasing to find out that something is wrong or turn a blind eye on suspicious activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: When renting out the premises, the property owners should know who the tenants are.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Some people may misuse other people's identities to conduct illegal activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Therefore, the property owner should conduct identity checks to verify that the person is who he claims to be.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Property agents must also go about their work professionally and do due diligence by helping to check on the identities of the potential tenants.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If they detect any suspicious transactions, they should inform the property owners and report to the Police.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As a community, we can also do our part to stop vice activities from taking root in the heartlands.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These syndicates were conducting their business on the Internet and some are even based overseas, as what the Senior Parliamentary Secretary has shared with us just now.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will they help us to round up those who are advertising sexual services from overseas?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do the anonymity clauses hinder investigations and, if so, do we need stronger laws in this respect?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I support firm action against home owners and tenants who knowingly let out their premises for vice activities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, I disagree that conducting identity checks at the point of signing lease agreements could be helpful in determining the tenant’s motives.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I note that CEA, property agencies and agents will be brought in to assist home owners and tenants to conduct due diligence checks.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is a commendable move that will help the less knowledgeable property owners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, a respectable local or foreigner with all their paperwork in order could rent the place and then lie low for the first few weeks of occupancy, before beginning their operations behind the backs of the property owners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some landlords might also be overseas and not be able to conduct checks.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is it fair to hold landlords responsible for tenants' actions under such circumstances?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In my opinion, it would be more meaningful for home owners and property agents to establish a communication channel with neighbours and managing agent, if any.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These people are better positioned to blow the whistle if anything is amiss.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is a common practice in places, such as Australia.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With freelance sex workers on the rise, it would also be necessary to extend the new regulations to any person who serves as their intermediary, regardless of whether the sex worker was procured to work as one.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should also examine the root of the issue.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is this purely because of increased accessibility of online platforms or are there other reasons?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What are the demographics of the people who use such services?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we do anything to educate these people about illegal prostitution and the risks involved?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin)  : 	This Bill proposes that if tenants conduct vice activities in the house, the landlord will also be held responsible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government and CEA will assist the landlords to check the tenant's background.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, even if the tenants have a clean record, they may still conduct vice activities in the premises afterwards.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, is it fair to hold the landlords responsible?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If something is not quite right in the house, the neighbours would be more likely to become aware of that.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, for home owners and property agents, having a communication channel with their neighbours and the managing agent can help deter vice activities more effectively.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill will allow the Police to better deal with overseas vice websites targeting Singapore and syndicates that bring women to Singapore to become sex workers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some chat apps, such as Telegram, have anonymous functions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will this deter the Police in their investigation efforts?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Here, I would like to thank the Government for their increased efforts to fight vice activities, especially in residential areas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This will allow our residents to enjoy a peaceful environment once again.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Names and addresses have been anonymised to maintain confidentiality.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: A lady with a young family living in a condominium came to see me at my Meet-the-People Session.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Seven months prior to this, she had noticed suspicious activities going on at a unit across from hers.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Both men and women were coming in at regular intervals throughout the afternoon, night and into the early hours of the morning.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They were not the same people as you and I would expect if they were members of the same family living in that unit.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They were of different ethnicities, different ages and some, as she described to me, would apparently seem to be under the influence of perhaps alcohol or drugs.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: She tried calling the authorities several times to assess.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But each time, she would get responses, such as, and I quote, "The Police have more urgent crime to fight.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And madam, we cannot arrest people unless you provide us with the hard evidence." And thus, her family installed a CCTV camera to get that hard evidence.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The Police asked for photos, evidence and facts, and it was documented with very good timeline annotation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Different people, different ages, different ethnic groups coming into that unit.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The pictures were very telling, very hard evidence, even better than the chat logs that were mentioned earlier.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Different faces, different people coming in individually or in twos or threes at approximately two to three hourly intervals.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But then it was taking so long and, in view of this, she came to see me.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: That was some half a year after all these had surfaced.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Neither her managing agent nor her Management Corporation Strata Title (MCST) could assist her.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Now, for fear of her family's safety, she finally decided to come forward.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: After all, the definition of "vice" by the Merriam-Webster dictionary is really "immoral or evil habit, a sinful or a criminal practice".

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This mother, with young children, living in a residential area, had genuine concerns.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I assisted her to sort out her issues, of course, and it is now settled.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But the point I am trying to make, Sir, is this: does it have to be so challenging for one young family and a concerned mom to activate the authorities for issues like this?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We want to make it a stern point and a deterrence.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They can provide the ears and eyes you so need.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is the best model to have for us to work to deprive the operating spaces in the heartlands and in the residential areas causing all the disamenities.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We have the policies, we have the framework, we have the guidelines, but there may be gaps in execution of these.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, good ground feedback is necessary and useful and can be very powerful, indeed, to ensure that we can execute these policies effectively.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Education alone will not get the results we desire.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Those involved are too entrenched, the education target may work perhaps for younger people who are considering venturing into this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: You may try to stop them using deterrent publicity, heightened awareness and education combined, but it has to be more persistent and more consistent.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Otherwise, we will not get the results that we started off to get.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: On the vice rates, for it to have impact, do more and make it regular, sustainable and consistent, for it to have the effect and the results that it is intended.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Otherwise, it will be a cat-and-mouse game, you leave and they will come out and play.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: You cannot imagine how challenging it is on the ground when feedback is given and it results in a cursory, standardised reply from the agencies or HDB.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These gaps need to be addressed and require absolute strengthening.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The authorities may need to look at these more wholesomely and this whole interdependent cycle and ring we need to break.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In the heartlands, coffee shops are one culprit area for these activities.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We have noticed blatant breaches, and overt activities related to vice at these coffee shops seem to be ongoing in broad daylight.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What else can one conjecture when dubious characters or so-called pimps sit at the corner table of a coffee shop the whole afternoon, into the night and the early hours of the morning and even after the coffee shop closes?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The same person with the same shirt, with the same characters around them.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They make negotiation for girls and many other things.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And it is very, very blatant and obvious to the lay person.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, responses from the authorities, such as "It is a public place and anyone can really sit there", are really not helping the situation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For online vice, it is even more challenging.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We are very connected as a society, given the number of devices each person possesses.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How are we able to work with overseas agencies and countries on this?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A cursory scan of some of our tabloids shows advertising for somewhat dubious outlets peddling health services and therapies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It does not take much to know that many health clubs and so-called massage parlours are but false fronts for vice activities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We see it in various parts of our island, especially in the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Darkened windows, heavy curtains, signages, instructions to go via the back entrance and somewhat under-dressed foreign ladies beckoning only to men to come in to relax.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are not hidden away in some private corner of our island or some back alleyway.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They exist right under the noses of authorities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some of our older malls like Chinatown and elsewhere have become centres of vice activities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To give an example, the basement of Katong Shopping Centre is a case in point – better known for chicken rice, banana pies and tailors – but also a warren of small stalls with ladies in heavy make-up cooing away at passers-by, with no regard for the sensitivities of those with younger children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some leave little to the imagination of the services that they prefer to provide, besides the purported advertising of physical therapy or facials.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is about time we take firmer action to weed them out from the heartlands and return decency to our living environments.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the last few years, I have also received feedback on vice activities occurring in our estates, both private and public housing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wish to ask the Ministry to work closely with the Ministry of National Development to advise MCSTs as well as how to work with HDB to ensure that vice activities do not end up right at the doorsteps of families, as pointed out by the two previous hon Members.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Sometimes, it is difficult even for the MCSTs and Managing Agents to decide how to deal with feedback and complaints of such matters.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To give one specific example, a private condo in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Residents long suspected that one unit in the block was involved in illegal vice activities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, there were very few levers available to them to try to obtain evidence despite reports to the Police.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It took some time before the issue was resolved.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some of the same frustration that the hon Member Prof Fatimah Lateef's residents have gone through are the same experiences perhaps elsewhere in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How does the Ministry then plan to identify and better prevent such premises from being used for prostitution?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many, as I had previously mentioned, operate with almost brazen impunity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How many does the Ministry estimate are currently operating and how will the enforcement be done?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the amendments to section 148(4) which places the burden of proof upon owners or agents of owners to prove that they could not be ascertained that the place is used as a brothel, how will the Ministry prevent loopholes that may well allow the masterminds behind such enterprises to escape the arm of the law?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It does not take much effort to search for such advertising.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is a sophisticated online advertising platform that was first founded in 2002.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The site lists everything from detailed services, districts, statistics, even so called "field reports" from customers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That alone should give us pause for thought on the value of this horrendous industry.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Back then, the Hong Kong Police declared a strategic victory over this biggest online vice site.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Its servers are now based in the US, and it has expanded its operations to advertise in 40 other countries besides Hong Kong, from Japan to even Bangladesh.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Their Hong Kong operations alone currently list 1,522 profiles across the Island, Peninsula and New Territories.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this game of cat and mouse, it is the mouse that can squirrel away easily and proliferate in various ways and forms.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, therefore, wish to ask how effective the Ministry thinks that the proposed amendments will be in rooting out the rats and clamping down on such nefarious forms of advertising.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is because while section 146A(1) will raise the penalties, the experience of Hong Kong seems to indicate that the penalties, in themselves, are not sufficient deterrence against those who seek to gain from exploiting women.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The global hosting of websites as well as the dark web have proven to make law enforcement more complex than before.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wish to also ask the Ministry to clarify the penalties as amended in the Women's Charter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At this point, I wish to share three stories from interviews over the years that have left me with much sorrow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Pearl is fair and of slight build, with almond-shaped eyes, she has masqueraded as a Japanese girl in Taipei.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She says she taught herself Japanese and watched YouTube to learn Japanese mannerisms and, in her words, "how to be more Kawaii".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She said that, in doing so, she can be a premium girl, fetching three times the price per customer than if she advertised herself as Chinese.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She is what is referred to in the industry as an outcall girl, clients will call up her agent after reviewing her profile on Line or WeChat and fix a time and location which she will go to.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She has been to Taiwan a few times and to Australia, too.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Each trip lasts two weeks and each time she makes US$3,000 to US$4,000, a princely sum back home.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When I asked her why she does it, she grins and says it is a quick way to make money at her age and she earns much much more than her peers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, despite that smile, she has no joy in her eyes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second girl is Rainbow, she hails from Thailand.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She was a regular Honey Girl in Hong Kong until she met an agent that abused her and other girls.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She used to make trips out to Hong Kong and, as a Honey Girl, will be booked into hotels in tourist districts and wait for calls to service men who will look her up via online adverts and make appointments through agents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She could never leave her hotel room during that time, eating just instant noodles and smoking cigarettes between customers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She claims that she saved the money she had for her parents back in the village and to pay for her younger brother's education.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She claimed to be doing sales overseas to her family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The money she had left over she undertook plastic surgery to become more attractive.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thinking she would benefit from a more aggressive agent who could bring in more well-paying clientele, she changed her pimp and was sent to a neighbouring resort island on the pretext of being an escort.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Instead, she found herself enslaved and locked up, servicing clients who roughed her up and her own agent who raped and beat her repeatedly over the course of three months.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Terrified and psychologically scarred, she has since been rescued, found it difficult to return to a normal life and also to return to her family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She was all of 19 when she was freed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When I met her, she would flinch at every sound, her eyes frenzied, darting back and forth as if frightened of shadows and of doors opening.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Here was a girl who might have had a future, someone's daughter, someone's sister, used, abused, left as an empty worn-out shell, her future cruelly torn from her.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are also many examples that I shared in 2014, when we debated the passing of the Prevention of Human Trafficking Bill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I met Mya, a 21-year-old girl from Mong La, Myanmar, in 2009.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Despite her youth, she had, at that time, the weight of the world on her and looked as if she was in her 40s.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She was born blind and was sold by her aunt to traffickers at the age of four.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She was rescued at the age of 16 – remember this, she was sold at the age of four – but her instinct then was to try to run back to her brothel and captors because it was the only reality, the only "home" that she knew.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a trade that we cannot and should never romanticise or glamourise.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A developed nation like ours that takes pride in the progress that our women and the progress that they have made and honours our mothers, sisters and wives, cannot possibly be proud to have men treat women and their bodies as mere commodities for carnal gratification.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of us in this House have daughters, too.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can we imagine a world where women are allowed to be exploited and abused as the same one that we hope our own daughters and sisters will grow up, thrive and succeed in?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will we lift our heads in the future and say to them that we stood by and closed one eye to what is nothing more than the commercialised rape of women?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That this safe and secure society that we take pride in – one that educates our girls, raises them up as a generation of leaders to hopefully change the world for the better and, yet, still allows dens of subjugation to exist amongst us?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yes, that is what the Charter is meant to do.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is an abhorrent activity and it is never a necessary evil.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not about management but about eradication, hopefully, soon.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It was just last month when I brought to the attention of this House in the Second Reading of the Income Tax Act that we still use archaic and deeply derogatory terms like "lunatic", "idiot" or "insane" to describe our differently-abled Singaporeans in our legislature.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And here we are, in section 144 of the Women's Charter and clause 7 of the amendments, we now call them "mentally defective"!

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I was not clear in my ask of the Minister for Finance with the Income Tax Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But I would like to be direct with my clarification with the Minister on this Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Now, back to the amendments to this Bill, Mr Speaker, notwithstanding my support for the Bill, I have two key clarifications to seek from the Minister.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, given that the Ministry acknowledges the exploitation that happens in the sex industry with these amendments, would it be more efficient and effective for us to also engage sex workers as part of the solution by encouraging and protecting them to come forward to report on these offenders?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A recent report recounts a man who facilitated Thai sex workers into Singapore and required the women to submit all their income for the first 20 customers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I also learnt about other examples of exploitation by agents from Project X, a non-governmental organisation (NGO) that was started 11 years ago by a social worker who saw how sex workers are amongst the most marginalised in our society and needed support; and The T Project, Singapore's first and only shelter for homeless transgender women, some of whom are also sex workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Jasmine came to Singapore to work on a six-month visa that allows her to do "free work" at the behest of her friend. "Free work" was the agent's way of expertly insinuating that she could do sex work anywhere in Singapore, even though the visa she had was to work as a performing artiste in a bar.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She was told it would cost her $15,000 in total which she must pay over the course of six months.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Three months later, Jasmine was arrested on the street.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At this point, she had already paid $6,900 to her agent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Desperate, Jasmine went to Project X who helped her lodge reports with both the Police and the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The agent and the employer have ostensibly violated the Women's Charter Article 142 on "importation of woman or girl by false pretences" as well as Article 146 on "persons living on or trading in prostitution".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, after multiple trips to the Police station, the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) and MOM, Jasmine was deported three weeks later on having committed the offence of not working at her designated workplace.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, the agent was still actively recruiting women based on the WhatsApp posts that Jasmine shared with Project X after she left Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In yet another case, a single mother with a seven-year-old son in her late 20s was arrested after a tip-off.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Rose assisted the Police in every way possible.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, the agent whom she never met in person, had covered up his tracks on WhatsApp with fake and inactive numbers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Rose had her passport taken away and given a Special Pass for the duration.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Project X alone supports about an average of eight of such exploitation cases every year for the last three years and none of these cases so far saw the agents nabbed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, it begs the question whether simply raising penalties will be adequate in curbing such abuse, especially for agents who know how to circumvent the law, who have intimate knowledge of the women's families and who leverage technology to conceal their identities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The National Institute of Justice, the research agency of the US Department of Justice, released a 2016 report that pointed out that the "certainty of being caught is a vastly more powerful deterrent than the punishment".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They make a clear distinction between incapacitation and deterrence.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Their evidence, which encompasses a large body of research on crime deterrence, suggests that higher penalties neither chasten already convicted criminals nor have the biggest effect on deterring potential crimes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, certainty, or "the likelihood of being caught and punished", is the major deterrent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This means that, in addition to raising penalties, we must also increase our precision in targeting and apprehending exploitative agents.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To increase precision in targeting agents, the most intuitive and economic way is to enlist their victims.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This makes the women under exploitative agents our most powerful ally.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The majority of women who go to Project X for support after exploitation refused to make a Police report because they fear that they will face punishment, deportation and blacklisting.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When our most efficient and effective access to exploitative agents is through the women they have abused, will the Minister work with the sex workers by concretising victim support as part of the solution?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Conditional immunity for sex workers specifically has been adopted in the American states of California and Utah.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: California's SB-233, which was passed just this year, echoes many concerns that we have in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: According to the official Senate floor analysis of SB-233, sex workers are victims of violent crime at a disproportionately high rate.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Because they fear criminal charges and mistreatment with the police, they rarely report crimes done to them.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This will not just increase the number of whistleblowers but also reinforce the Bill's intent to protect vulnerable women and bring the offenders to justice.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Criminal compensation will further improve our precision in targeting exploitation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Women who enter into arrangements with unlicensed agents are almost always in a very low socio-economic position and, therefore, desperate for work opportunities to survive and support their families.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that the prosecution and investigation officer can invest greater effort in helping the victims understand their rights, produce evidence to guide compensation liabilities and collaborate with the Court to ensure the agents make these payments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This would increase the incentive for abused women to report their agents while also effectively protecting the interest of already-exploited victims.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, experts have demonstrated that a framework that recognises the safety and welfare of sex workers elevates the safety of all women and makes it easier for those who have been exploited to leave the sex industry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The alternative, however, is that exploitative agents and sexual predators continue to act with impunity and so more women are preyed on to join the industry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We need to see sex workers as part of the solution, including our transgender sex workers, who are also sometimes victims to exploitative and abusive agents.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We still have a biased cultural attitude towards the sex industry, one that legitimises men’s persistent demand for sexual services but villianises the women who supply these services.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, the CEDAW Committee has recognised sex workers as a group of women who are disproportionately affected by gendered violence, discrimination and marginalisation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: CEDAW's approach to gender equality should inform any policy to protect sex workers from exploitation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must involve and empower sex workers as equal partners and experts in determining the solutions that work for them.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The physical, emotional and sexual violence that are systematically perpetrated against sex workers undermine gender equality.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Studies have found that sexual violence is likely to occur more commonly in cultures that foster beliefs of perceived male superiority and social and cultural inferiority of women.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At a time when a group like SG Nasi Lemak exists, when peeping tom upskirting cases are on a steady rise, it is paramount that we treat all forms of gender-based violence with urgency and gravity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We should, therefore, be hyper-vigilant of the normalising effects of impunity for exploitative agents and employers and do all we can to prevent the disenfranchisement of sex workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I befriended a sex worker almost 15 years ago.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She shared with me that it was the sheer desperation of poverty back home that drove her to be a sex worker here so as to feed her son and two ailing parents back home.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lily eventually left the sex trade after having saved enough to take courses.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She is now a world-travelling and well-respected professional in the hair and beauty trade.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Sex workers may be looked down upon, but it is clear that many of them have much to contribute to society and also, like us, dream for a better life.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Not being heard as a sex worker is no reason for silence when it comes to being exploited.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When we offer protection and give them a voice to be part of the solution to the problems of abuse and oppression that we are trying to solve in the sex industry, Mr Speaker, I am sure they will come forward to say, #MeToo.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will resume the Sitting at 3.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.35 pm until 3.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government's approach has been to restrict prostitution to licensed brothels by outlawing activities like solicitation and pimping that are largely linked to unlicensed prostitution.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This model has generally worked in the past to limit such vice-related activities to certain areas of Singapore where licensed brothels operate.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This approach, however, is less likely to work in today's context where commercial sex can be procured easily online via the Internet and social media platforms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Operators of online commercial sex platforms have increasingly offered sexual services out of residential units, such as private apartments, condominiums and even from HDB flats in the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: According to a news article published in The Straits Times in 2017, operators of these unlicensed brothels are attracted by the low rent of these residential units, as well as the discreet locations that these residential units have.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A follow-up Straits Times article in May 2019 reported how more than 150 women and a man were arrested in May for vice-related activities that were operating out of residential units, some of which were in the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Operating out of an unlicensed brothel compromises the safety and security of an environment in which young children and families live, and I am heartened to know that the amendments in this Bill comprise active measures to ensure that landlords are now legally obliged to not turn a blind eye to such activities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am supportive of this amendment and its enhanced penalties as they would help to restrict the use of residential units as unlicensed brothels by putting the onus on property owners and their appointed agents to not turn a blind eye to illicit vice activities conducted on their premises.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, I am encouraged that the amendments also offer protection to owners and agents who have done their due diligence and are genuinely unaware of the happenings in their units.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In short, those who have done their due diligence should not be unjustly punished.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given that such services can be managed and organised by overseas vice syndicates, there are, indeed, merits in extending the enforcement power of the authorities beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, the challenge lies in actually being able to enforce the law.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How would the authorities carry out cross-border enforcement actions against overseas-based vice-related operations, especially in contexts where Singapore does not have repatriation or reciprocal arrangements with the countries where the syndicates are operating out of?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Government would shed some light on this area.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the law punishes the offenders, I believe more can be done to support unwitting victims who have been deceived by these vice syndicates.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of these women and girls were lured to come to Singapore by false promises of legitimate employment but only to be coerced and trapped into sex work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of them were desperate to leave the trade but were coerced to stay in the trade with threats.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Government's position is not to prosecute potential victims of trafficking, I hear that we need to put in place a better support system to rescue these women from vice syndicates.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Government and authorities work with local NGOs to put in support systems for these victims before we repatriate them?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Government also work with the respective agencies in the victims' home countries to ensure that their welfare is addressed before we send them back, as they might have to face possible recrimination from the vice syndicates in their home country?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Doing so will equip our Police Force more adequately as criminals are exploiting technology to boost their revenue and protect themselves by operating their illegal businesses remotely.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Certainly, owners and tenants who allow such activities to be conducted on their premises should be severely punished.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The law requires owners to perform due diligence when leasing out their properties, such as but not limited to, conducting identity checks when signing the lease agreements.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the tenants who had been cleared under such checks could still use the residences to conduct illegal activities without the owner's knowledge.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are prostitutes who enter Singapore as tourists or on visit passes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some individuals operate on their own while others are flown in and controlled by crime syndicates overseas or even locally.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we prevent these syndicates from engaging in such activities in our homeland?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most importantly, we need to protect those who are abused and trafficked here for such exploitation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do not doubt that there is a need to curb vice activities perpetuated through online platforms and I agree that this is a serious concern that must be addressed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also support MHA’s intent to deprive vice syndicates of operating space, especially in the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My residents and myself included all want a sense of safety and security where we live.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But while I support these amendments, I have concerns about their effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are we addressing only the symptoms of the issue and not the root cause?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first concern is about the amendment targeting the irresponsible lease of premises and whether it is feasible and practical.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: None of us wants our neighbourhoods to become hubs of vice activities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But my question is: how are home owners and tenants supposed to enforce this?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One way of satisfying themselves is to conduct identity checks at the point of signing their lease agreements, as part of due diligence when renting out or subletting their premises.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In practice, however, how does a home owner or tenant perform "reasonable diligence" other than asking directly whether one is a sex worker?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the home owner or tenant drops by and find that the tenant or subtenant is having sex with another person, how do they determine whether or not that is a vice activity?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the Minister can provide clarity on how we will be enforcing this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second concern is about whether our attempts to clamp down on sexual services work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2010, Member of Parliament Mr Baey Yam Keng said that vice raids in Geylang led to pimps and prostitutes "spilling out" of the area.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Former Nominated Member of Parliament Kok Heng Leun raised the same concerns in his speech on the Massage Establishments Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He said, "In the past, there used to be these health centres where sexual services were provided alongside massage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most of these health centres were not allowed to renew their licences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The shutdown of these health centres led to the proliferation of smaller parlours set up by the people who used to work at these health centres.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we wipe out one area, we only push the sex workers to another area which we then try to wipe out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that vice activities will always evolve, and enforcement needs to evolve as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I met up with Singaporean sex workers when I was researching the Massage Establishment Bill and I met up with Singaporean sex workers again when researching this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I sat there listening to their stories, their fears and their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are fellow Singaporeans and many are victims of circumstance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many feel that they have no choice but to be sex workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to ask ourselves how many people would willingly sell sexual services?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I listened to one woman share about how she got kicked out of her house by her parents when she was young, became homeless, did not know where to go for help and, ultimately, entered the sex trade just to survive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She was beaming with pride when she informed everyone during the dialogue that she had just paid the deposit for a make-up course and everyone in the room cheered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I listened to how another woman became a sex worker when she was only 19 years old and has been doing this for four years now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her parents divorced when she was five years old and both parents did not want her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She was left with her grandmother who raised her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For her entire childhood, she was constantly reminded that she had no parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I cannot imagine the impact that had on a young child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She did not do well in her studies and could not get into a polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She tried to enrol in a private polytechnic but did not have enough money to pay the tuition fees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She then tried to get a bank loan but failed as she could not find a guarantor.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not knowing where else to go for help, she ultimately entered the sex trade for money to fund her education.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can all take the moral high ground and tell the sex workers that they know the risk of sex work and that they can find another job, so why should we protect them and help them?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I hope we remember that these are fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Rather than judge them for their actions, I hope we can help them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Women’s Charter is all about protecting women and girls from exploitation and harm and this should include sex workers as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The recent case where three youths hatched a plot to rob sex workers at knifepoint highlights how sex workers are especially vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The trio agreed on this plot as this would be the "safest" way to commit a crime as they would be preying on the sex workers’ "vulnerabilities and insecurities", given the illicit nature of their work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The sex workers I spoke to feared that when they report a crime committed against them, they, too, will be arrested because of the illicit nature of their work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, many do not report the crime, and my concerns are not just for the sex workers but also for society at large.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have people committing crimes and getting away with it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They might continue with their crimes and start targeting others or, worse still, evolve to committing more serious crimes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Do we really want a rapist to get away scot-free just because his victim is a sex worker?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does our society become a safer place for all if this continues?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I can understand that what I am proposing is not a simple suggestion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MHA look into this holistically to assess the pros and cons of such laws and see what effects they have had on society?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, many of the sex workers I spoke to said they wanted to leave the sex industry but needed help doing so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Studies have showed that women who want to leave the sex work industry are trapped in their industry due to two key factors: one, society's prejudice against former sex workers; and two, the women’s lack of social support and low self-esteem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The programme aims to help sex workers who wish to leave the industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Over six months, case workers work with the women to devise a customised plan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The plan aims to help the women in five important ways: financial planning, individual counselling, job skills training, family counselling, and social and communication skills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the end of the six months, the women will have the option of continuing or exiting the programme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not an easy transition, but the result, I believe, is worth the effort.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Criminalising prostitution only drives such activities underground, resulting in crime syndicates taking control over such activities." There is a need for us to rethink and relook our policies and remember what our former Minister told us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that rather than just prosecute sex workers, we can provide help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Rather than entrap them with our undercover officers, we can engage them holistically.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Rather than lecture them on morals and the law, we can listen to them and understand why they became a sex worker, what their concerns are and what their aspirations are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that MHA will consider holding discussions with the sex workers directly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would be keen to help with this and facilitate it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
