text: Some sex workers may be concerned about meeting with MHA for fear of being identified, but we can start by meeting with sex workers who are transiting out of the industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us work together with them to find long-term solutions rather than against them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But let us remember that they are also someone’s child, someone's daughter, someone's loved one and, more than anything, these are fellow Singaporeans who need help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And by helping them transit out of the sex industry, we might actually reduce the number of Singaporean sex workers much faster than arresting them and playing this cat-and-mouse game.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over the past few years, illegal vice activities have been popping up in HDB precincts, causing disamenities in the neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of these elderly residents may not be well educated and may not know what their legal obligations are as a landlord.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such, I have three questions for MHA.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would they be deemed to have done their duty as long as they carry out the checks as advised by the property agents?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Third, for elderly residents who may have mobility issues, can they rely on the property agents to carry out the necessary checks?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such, I hope MHA can give clarifications on my questions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I do have a few questions and suggestions for the Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed amendments to the Women’s Charter are timely as the sex trade in Singapore has been evolving in tandem with new technologies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a former Police commander, I have seen firsthand how illegal vice activities have moved from brothels masquerading under the guise of massage parlours, to online messaging applications like WeChat which utilise geotargeting technologies to allow anyone to find sex workers in their vicinity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The confluence of the popularity of such messaging platforms and the rise in short-term rentals, perpetuated by platforms like AirBnB, will increase the difficulty of enforcement against vice syndicates.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through short-term rental platforms, syndicates now have easy access to a large inventory of locations that they can hop around to offer prostitution services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My suspicion is that many are operating out of apartments rented on a short-term basis, to avoid detection.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, while I am supportive of the proposed amendments to tackle irresponsible leasing of premises for vice activities, this only deals with home owners who legally rent out their premises.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How will our Police Officers enforce against the syndicates that tap on illegal short-term rental platforms to offer vice activities?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Messaging platforms are also introducing new technologies that will make it harder for our anti-vice officers to catch vice syndicates.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The recent furore over the SG Nasi Lemak chat group has exposed the use of Telegram as an encrypted messaging platform, used to disseminate both obscene and pornographic content, including the offer of sexual services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Telegram also has a "self-destruct" feature, which users can set their messages, photos and files to be deleted on both the sender and the recipients’ devices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To deter people from committing such offences, could the Senior Parliamentary Secretary provide a concrete example of when a person based overseas would be in breach of the new section 146A, and how would the Ministry act against such a person who is not physically in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While we tackle the rise of vice activities perpetuated through new media, it is vital that we continue to take action against the business operations of unsavoury establishments that masquerade as public entertainment outlets in residential areas, especially those with young children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: During my time with the Clementi Police Division, my officers regularly took enforcement actions against the massage parlours suspected to be offering illegal sex services in mixed-use developments, such as Bukit Timah Shopping Centre.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But despite our constant enforcement actions, seedy establishments continued to operate – many times out of the same shop unit – as syndicates were able to find locals to register themselves as new owners of the massage parlours and act as their fall guy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In our colloquial terms, we term this as "finding a tua pek kong".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Now, as a Member of Parliament, I receive regular complaints from residents about the seedy public entertainment and massage outlets located in mixed developments, such as Orchard Towers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Members would agree with me that such seedy businesses should not be co-located in residential areas, especially those with young children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How would the new definition of "brothel" and the amendments to section 148 tackle the "tua pek kong" phenomenon and eradicate such seedy public entertainment and massage outlets in mixed-use developments?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry also consider imposing a cap on the number of such outlets in a specified area, particularly in areas where there are many residences?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a point that I have raised before here in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From my policing experience, I have often noticed that once an area has reached a certain threshold of such outlets, syndicates tend to gravitate towards the area as their next business opportunity, resulting in a quick surge of illegal vice activities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, while we pit our wits against these syndicates, it is vital that our anti-vice officers recognise the shift in such trends, which are abetted by new encrypted messaging technologies and short-term rental platforms.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also urge more enforcement action to be done to ensure that such seedy businesses are not co-located in mixed-use residential developments, where there are many young children residing.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I shall first address the broader questions on the Government’s policy on managing vice, before going into questions relating to specific amendments in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, regarding the Government's policy on vice and our vice management strategy.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if these amendments will only drive vice elsewhere, further underground.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Alex Yam gave a passionate argument for the abolition of prostitution altogether in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Alex Yam shared that we should eradicate the exploitation of women, instead of management.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, as Nominated Member Anthea Ong pointed out, the economic and social factors, such as poverty and a lack of realistic career options that push women into prostitution, will not go away by criminalising prostitution.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: She pointed out that sex workers, and empowering these women, can instead be part of the solution.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We studied the approaches adopted by various countries.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Some ban the purchase and selling of sex, others focus on criminalising demand and yet others have chosen to decriminalise or legalise the sex industry.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I acknowledge Mr Louis Ng's concerns about syndicates which will continue to evolve alongside changes to our laws and our enforcement efforts.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Where that line is crossed, the Government must intervene to safeguard our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This intervention is part of our larger vice management strategy, which Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Alex Yam and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We also remind residents to be vigilant against vice activities by working with partners, such as HDB and CEA, to promote awareness among residents and property agents, and raising deterrence against vice activities by publicising Police's enforcement efforts.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Downstream, ICA and the Police conduct raids on premises suspected of harbouring immigration offenders and vice activities; and the Police also conduct joint operations with their overseas counterparts, to target the upper echelons of these syndicates.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I gave an example of such a joint operation with our counterparts in China in my earlier speech.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members also had questions about these downstream enforcement practices.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I appreciate the concerns faced by the resident in the example shared by Prof Fatimah Lateef.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police do, indeed, hope to work with eyes and ears on the ground, be it vigilant property owners, tenants or property agents, to aid ongoing investigations or uncover unreported crime.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police may not appear to respond immediately to all information received, but this is also because they will have to verify the information before conducting any enforcement action.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But I assure Members that the Police value every piece of information provided by members of the public.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The amendments today also demonstrate our commitment to weed out vice syndicates from residential areas.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There are many channels available for the public to provide such information, including lodging a Police report or using iWitness.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The same goes for sex workers who are victims of crime.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Anthea Ong, through her examples, also made a broader point about a perception that syndicates are getting away scot-free, in spite of sex workers coming forward to assist with Police investigations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police will follow up on information provided by sex workers, but as explained in my earlier speech, syndicates are finding ways to evade detection.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This means that in some cases, the Police may find it challenging to identify the agents or to establish the culpability of persons involved.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And this is why we need these amendments in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police update their enforcement strategies to remain effective.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, they also conduct "precision" operations, to quote Ms Anthea Ong, targeted at the upper echelons of the syndicates.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, there is a broad spectrum of enforcement operations conducted by the Police: regular, sustained enforcement raids targeting vices in the heartlands, and precise strikes to disrupt the syndicates.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members of Parliament Mr Melvin Yong and Prof Fatimah Lateef asked about the vice situation at areas, such as Orchard Towers and Geylang.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police have adopted a targeted enforcement strategy at these locations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Broadly, they keep a high enforcement and operations tempo at these locations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Depending on the ground issues, the Police also work with other enforcement agencies and community stakeholders to detect and deter illegal activities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I mentioned that we have in place a regulatory regime for massage establishments and public entertainment outlets, as part of our vice management strategy.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is outside of the scope of the amendments, but I will briefly talk about the principles.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police take into consideration the Urban Redevelopment Authority's planning intent, the law and order situation of an area, and the operators’ background, before issuing licences to these operators.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The operators have to comply with the licensing conditions, which include ensuring no immoral activity is carried out in the premises, and the Police conduct regular enforcement checks on the outlets.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Errant operators may face regulatory sanctions or even criminal penalties under the relevant legislation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Anthea Ong, Mr Alex Yam and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked for some vice-related statistics.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The number of "pop-up brothels" in operation is difficult to estimate with certainty but suffice to say that it is on an upward trend.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We do not collect data on persons who purchase sexual services, as this is not an offence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So far, I have set out our law enforcement strategies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I now turn to the issue of protection and support for sex workers, which Ms Anthea Ong, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Darryl David spoke about.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have tough laws against trafficking-in-persons, under the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act (PHTA).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There are safe reporting channels available to victims.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Persons can report to the Police or MOM via their hotlines and websites or call 999 if immediate Police assistance is required.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We also have in place a victim care framework, which includes providing assistance with temporary accommodation, food, counselling services, medical care and temporary employment.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Sex workers should not keep silent if they have been abused or exploited.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Any sex worker who is a victim of crime should come forward and get the Police's assistance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police will look into all allegations of criminal offences.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Support is available for prosecution witnesses, such as assistance with housing and employment.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Melvin Yong cited the report by the US State Department regarding trafficking-in-persons.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The report misrepresents the ground realities of the trafficking situation here.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA issued a clarification published in the Straits Times in July this year.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Of the 16 alleged trafficking cases, 10 were alleged to be sex trafficking.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA has also clarified this with the US directly.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Anthea Ong also asked about criminal compensation for sex workers who have been victims of crime.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As Ms Anthea Ong has highlighted, there is already an existing legal framework under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Under the law, compensation is a matter for the Courts to consider.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Where appropriate cases are brought to the attention of the Police by the victim, the Police will highlight to the Attorney-General Chambers to consider making such a case on behalf of the victim.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Regarding conditional immunity for prosecution witnesses suggested by Ms Anthea Ong and Mr Louis Ng, this is an issue that needs further deliberation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will have to take into account, holistically, the circumstances and actions of the sex worker and prevailing laws and policies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Women's Charter is meant to protect women in general, including sex workers, from being exploited by pimps.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police have not prosecuted any sex workers for sex work, as prostitution is not an offence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, foreigners who work as sex workers in Singapore have also violated the conditions of their entry into Singapore and are considered prohibited immigrants under our law.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will thus have to carefully consider the impact of granting immunity to such individuals on public safety and our criminal justice system as a whole.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Ng also shared about helping women transit out of sex work.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Community partners do play an important role in helping Singaporean sex workers, be it in helping them transit out of sex work or providing social support to them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Government will support such efforts where possible.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But we must also recognise that most sex workers are foreigners, and foreigners who are prostitutes in Singapore would have flouted our immigration laws.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Again, we have to carefully consider the impact of our policies on public safety and law and order.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I will next address Members' queries on specific clauses in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Darryl David and Mr Melvin Yong asked how the extraterritorial application of section 146A would be used in practice to target offenders based overseas.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah said the anonymity offered by some of these platforms could hinder investigations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If they are in a country with which Singapore has a Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT) or extradition treaty, it may be possible to seek their assistance for investigation or send an extradition request to the country, if this is practical or expedient.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Even if there are no formal reciprocal agreements, the Police will work with our foreign counterparts to share information and conduct joint enforcement and investigation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: While we acknowledge that extraterritorial laws have their limitations, the amendments to section 146A will still be an improvement over what we have today.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I explained the need for these amendments in my earlier speech.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To ascertain the identity of these offenders, the Police can rely on section 20 of the Criminal Procedure Code to order the production of any document or thing necessary for investigations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police also work with their overseas counterparts to share relevant information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I have just set out how the Police will rely on the amended section 146A to go after syndicate members overseas.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The other amendment to section 146A is to allow the Police to go after syndicate members in Singapore, even if they use a remote communication service based overseas.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The amended section 146A is not only applicable to syndicate members overseas.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Melvin Yong and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the use of social media and social messaging platforms to advertise the provision of sexual services in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Most syndicates rely instead on dedicated websites, such as SGWolves, which was taken down last year.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Many social media platforms have community standards and processes for users to report such posts to the company for take-down.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We thank Mr Gan Thiam Poh for his suggestion to require Internet intermediaries, such as social media providers, to do more to combat vice on their platforms proactively.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA is also working with other Government agencies to study the issue.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In doing so, we are seeking to find the right balance between our public safety outcomes, without imposing requirements that are unreasonably onerous on companies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In any case, such platforms are considered "remote communication services" under section 146A.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Anthea Ong and Mr Alex Yam asked if the higher maximum fines would be enough to deter the offenders.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The higher maximum fines are part of a broader suite of amendments to better deter vice syndicates.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Bill also raises the maximum jail terms, and penalties for reoffending.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Taken as a whole, this sends a strong signal to vice syndicates regarding the seriousness of the offence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Additionally, the prosecution can also apply to confiscate vice earnings under the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act (CDSA), and we have done so in the past.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Several Members asked whether the identity checks, as a form of reasonable diligence, would be effective in deterring syndicates from renting premises for vice activities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Some said identity checks, by themselves, may not be helpful in determining the tenant’s motives, and asked if it would be fair to hold landlords responsible for tenants' subsequent actions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But the tenant or occupier could be prosecuted for an offence of keeping, managing or assisting in the management of a brothel; the Bill does not amend or abolish this offence in section 148 subsection (1).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And where the tenant is not directly managing or keeping the brothel, the tenant cannot escape criminal liability unless he or she can show that he or she had no knowledge and could not, with reasonable diligence, have ascertained, that the premises are used as a brothel.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We had considered imposing post-transaction requirements, such as spotchecks on the unit, installing CCTVs, or checking with the neighbours.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We consulted a wide range of stakeholders on this and the general consensus was that it would be too onerous to impose legal obligations on property owners to implement post-transaction checks at this juncture.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Stakeholders said property owners or master tenants faced practical limitations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, as leases or sub-leases usually require them to respect the tenant's or subtenant's right to quiet enjoyment, it would be challenging to conduct surprise checks if the tenant or subtenant was not around to allow the inspection.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The owner or master tenant might arrange the inspection in advance, but this would defeat the purpose of the checks since syndicates will remove any evidence of illegal activity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And as Mr Louis Ng highlighted, the owner or master tenant may not be able to determine whether the place is used as a brothel.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There were also concerns about potential risks to the personal safety of the person conducting the checks, if crime syndicates are involved in the running of brothels out of these rented premises.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As Mr Darryl David and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah said, those who have done their reasonable diligence should not be unjustly punished.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The proposed approach in the Bill for owners and master tenants to exercise reasonable diligence at the point of entering into tenancy agreements is not too onerous and is something that many are already doing today.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As I said in my earlier speech, this amendment is also intended to get property owners and tenants started in asking the right questions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These will help deter syndicates attempting to misuse another person’s identity documents in order to rent a place to be used as a brothel.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing asked if property owners can rely fully on property agents’ advice and to carry out the checks for them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In my earlier speech, I also talked about the disciplinary action that property agents could be liable for, if they were found to have behaved negligently.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Property agents are allowed to conduct checks on behalf of property owners who are unable to meet the prospective tenants in person, for example, landlords who are overseas, or elderly landlords who may not be ambulant.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Apart from property agents, trusted parties, such as a family member, can also conduct these checks on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, an owner is ultimately responsible for the lease of his own property.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Owners who rely on third parties to check should verify that the checks have been completed satisfactorily, before entering into the lease agreement or allowing the prospective tenant to occupy the property.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: While property agents have a professional duty to advise their clients to the best of their abilities, and indeed most of them do so, the property owner should also be asking the right questions and satisfy himself or herself that the unit is being rented out in a responsible manner.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In addition, there are rules in place regarding the illegal or unauthorised use of premises for short-term accommodation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Property owners may also be liable for an offence under the Planning Act.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Just as Prof Fatimah Lateef, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Alex Yam said, property owners, tenants and property agents are our "eyes and ears" on the ground.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These amendments are part of our efforts to promote better collaboration with the community to remain vigilant against vice activities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Neighbours, managing agents and security guards are also part of this larger community.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We encourage the community to keep vigilant and report suspicious activities to the Police.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Because in Singapore, we do the same for the vice of drugs and we do so with much pride.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Banning drugs has not meant that we have completely eradicated them from our society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: But we have reduced the nefarious effects that come with these, such as violent crime, gangsterism and organised crime.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: As we have heard from many Members, many would not have willingly entered this trade.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Having been involved in work in the welfare of sex workers in the region, what we can do to uplift a lot of communities is perhaps the most important part and there are a lot of levers that Singapore as a developed country can do.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: At the end of the day, prostitution is no more than a repetitive round of sex acts.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I hope that the Ministry can consider some of these for future legislation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As I mentioned earlier, the experiences in other countries – the Member mentioned Sweden – have been mixed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There is no consensus as to whether laws that criminalise demand for paid sex actually decrease the actual demand for sex.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I think the Senior Parliamentary Secretary mentioned that it is harder to grant immunity when there are immigration offences as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So, can we look into at least granting immunity when there are no immigration offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Second, my call about funding for the next step programme, which is about helping Singaporean sex workers transit out of the industry, I think that is a much better way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Rather than keep trying to arrest them, we help them to get out of the industry, which will reduce the number of sex workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Third is whether MHA is open to having a closed dialogue with the sex workers themselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Hear from them directly and see how we can work together to address some of the concerns that MHA has.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But for the foreign sex workers, they have committed an immigration offence and that is why they have to be deported.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the last point on a dialogue, the Police, when they do come into contact with the sex workers, they do interact with them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But if he feels that there is a way for us to work even closer with voluntary welfare organisations to engage the sex workers, we will be happy to work with the Member further on this.
